learn.b: Every C# program starts running at a method called Main. Inside it you can write statements, and each statement ends with a semicolon. Console.WriteLine prints text and then moves to a new line.
Console lives in the System namespace, so we write using System; at the top of the file. Console.WriteLine prints a line, and Console.Write prints without a new line afterwards.

Curly braces { } group code into blocks. A comment starts with // and is ignored by the computer. Use comments to explain your code to humans. C# is case sensitive, so console and Console are different.
learn.code:
// This line is ignored
Console.WriteLine("Run"); // so is this part

learn.b: Console.ReadLine() waits for the user to type a line and gives it back as text (a string). You can store it in a variable and print it later. Newer C# versions also allow top-level statements, where you skip Main, but Main is what you will see in most books.

learn.b: A variable is a named box that holds a value. In C# you must say its type when you create it. The type decides what kind of value fits inside.

int holds whole numbers, double holds decimals, bool holds true or false, char holds one character in single quotes, and string holds text in double quotes. Use float or long when you need those sizes, and write f after a float number like 1.5f.
learn.code:
long big = 5000000000L;
float speed = 1.5f;

learn.b: The word var lets the compiler work out the type from the value, but the type is still fixed afterwards. A const is a value that can never change. Names usually start with a lowercase letter and use camelCase.
An int fits into a double automatically. Going the other way loses the decimals, so you must cast with (int). To turn text into a number use int.Parse or Convert.ToInt32.

learn.b: C# has + - * / and % (remainder). When both numbers are int, division also gives an int and drops the decimals. If one of them is a double, you get a decimal answer.
learn.code:
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2);    // 3
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2.0);  // 3.5
Console.WriteLine(7 % 2);    // 1

learn.b: x += 3 means x = x + 3. There are also -=, *=, /=. The ++ operator adds 1 and -- subtracts 1. These are very common in loops.
Comparisons give a bool. Use == to check equal, != for not equal, and < > <= >= for order. A single = is assignment, not comparison.
Combine bools with && (and), || (or) and ! (not). && is true only if both sides are true. || is true if at least one side is true. Parentheses make the order clear.
learn.code:
bool ok = (age > 12) && (age < 20);
bool no = !ok;

learn.b: A string is a sequence of characters. Use + to join strings, and .Length to count characters. Characters have positions starting at 0, so name[0] is the first one.
learn.code:
string s = "Hello";
Console.WriteLine(s.Length); // 5
Console.WriteLine(s[0]);     // H
Console.WriteLine(s + "!"); // Hello!

learn.b: Put a $ before the opening quote and write variables inside curly braces. This is the easiest way to build text from values. You can even put small expressions inside the braces.

ToUpper and ToLower change case. Contains checks for a piece of text. Replace swaps text. Substring cuts out part of a string. Strings are immutable, so these methods return a new string and do not change the original.
learn.code:
string t = "cat";
Console.WriteLine(t.ToUpper());      // CAT
Console.WriteLine(t.Contains("a")); // True
Console.WriteLine(t.Replace("c","b")); // bat

learn.b: Inside a string, \n means a new line and \" puts a quote mark in the text. Compare strings with ==. Use string.IsNullOrEmpty(s) to check for empty text.
learn.code:
Console.WriteLine("Line1\nLine2");
bool same = "a" == "a"; // true

learn.b: An if statement runs a block only when its condition is true. The condition must be a bool and goes in parentheses. Add else if for more choices and else for everything left over.
Use && and || to test several things at once. Only the first matching branch in an if chain runs. Remember to compare with == and not a single =.
A switch compares one value against many fixed cases. Each case ends with break. The default case runs when nothing else matches. It is neater than a long else if chain.

condition ? a : b picks a when the condition is true and b when it is false. It is a short way to choose between two values. Modern C# also has switch expressions, but the classic switch is what you meet first.
learn.code: string r = score >= 50 ? "pass" : "fail";

learn.b: A while loop repeats its block as long as the condition is true. Make sure something inside changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
A for loop packs the start, the condition and the step in one line, separated by semicolons. It is perfect when you know how many times to repeat.
foreach goes through every item of a collection one by one. A do-while loop always runs at least once because it checks the condition at the end.
break leaves the loop at once. continue skips the rest of this round and jumps to the next one. Loops can be nested, with one loop inside another, to make grids and tables.

qs.q: Which loop is best when you know how many times to repeat?
qs.why: for puts counter, condition and step together.

qs.q: Which loop always runs its body at least once?

learn.b: An array stores a fixed number of items of the same type. You choose its size when you create it. Items are reached with an index in square brackets, and the first index is 0.
You can fill an array right away with curly braces. The Length property tells you how many items it holds. The last valid index is Length - 1, and going outside gives an error at run time.
Use a for loop with the index when you need positions. Use foreach when you only need the values. Array.Sort and Array.Reverse change the order of the items in place.
A two dimensional array is like a table with rows and columns. You write int[,] and reach a cell with two indexes. Arrays have a fixed size, so for lists that grow you will later use List.

learn.b: A method is a named block of code you can run many times. You write the return type, the name, and parameters in parentheses. void means the method returns nothing. Inside a simple program the methods are marked static.
Parameters are inputs to the method. The return keyword sends a value back to the caller, and the return type must match it. Method names usually start with a capital letter in C#.

A parameter can have a default value, which makes it optional. You can also name the arguments when calling, so the order does not matter. Methods with the same name but different parameters are called overloads.

Normally a method gets a copy of simple values. The ref keyword passes the variable itself so the method can change it, and out lets a method give back extra results. Variables created inside a method only exist inside that method, which is called local scope.

learn.b: A class is a blueprint, and an object is one thing built from it. Fields store data and methods describe what the thing can do. You create an object with the new keyword.
A constructor is a special method with the same name as the class and no return type. It runs when you use new and sets up the object. The this keyword means the current object.

A property looks like a field but is controlled by get and set. The short form { get; set; } makes C# create the hidden field for you. Use private set to let only the class change the value. Properties protect your data, an idea called encapsulation.

public members can be used anywhere, private ones only inside the class. A static member belongs to the class itself, not to one object, like Console.WriteLine. Fields are usually private and exposed through properties.

learn.b: A class can inherit from another with a colon. The child class gets all the public members of the parent and can add its own. This avoids repeating code. C# allows only one parent class.

Mark a parent method virtual to allow children to replace it. The child uses override. When you call the method on a Dog stored in an Animal variable, the Dog version runs. This is polymorphism. Use base to call the parent version.

An abstract class cannot be created with new. It can contain abstract methods that have no body, and every child must override them. Use it for ideas like Shape that only make sense as specific shapes.
An interface lists members a class promises to have. Names usually start with I. A class can implement many interfaces. Interfaces let different classes be used in the same way.

learn.b: A List grows and shrinks, unlike an array. The T in angle brackets is the type of the items. Add appends, Remove deletes, and Count gives the size. You need using System.Collections.Generic; at the top.
A Dictionary stores pairs of a key and a value. You look up a value by its key, and every key must be unique. TryGetValue and ContainsKey check safely whether a key exists.

foreach works with lists and with dictionaries. For a dictionary each item is a KeyValuePair with Key and Value properties. Do not add or remove items while looping over a collection, or you get an error.

LINQ gives short ways to query collections. Add using System.Linq; to use it. Where filters, Select transforms, Sum, Max and Count calculate, and ToList turns the result into a list. The arrow => builds a small function called a lambda.

learn.b: An exception is an error that happens while the program runs, like dividing by zero. Put risky code in a try block. If it fails, the matching catch block runs instead of crashing the program.
A finally block always runs, even after an error, so it is good for cleanup. You can raise your own exception with throw. Catch the specific exception first and the general Exception last.

In Unity a C# class inherits from MonoBehaviour. Unity calls special methods for you: Start runs once at the beginning and Update runs every frame. A public field shows up in the Inspector, where you can change it without code.

Components are scripts and parts attached to a GameObject. GetComponent finds another component, and Debug.Log writes to the Console. Time.deltaTime is the time of one frame, which keeps movement the same on slow and fast computers.

qs.q: Which block holds code that might fail?
qs.why: Risky code goes in try.

qs.q: Which block always runs, error or not?
qs.why: finally is for cleanup.

qs.why: Start runs once; Update runs every frame.
